The #3 valve spring was found under the design minimum length and should be planned for replacement during the next outage (PN# 101A751YE-1). The V1 steam chest stem bushing and seat bores were found in poor conditions. Both areas were found oversized and out-or-round. The V1 valve is the first line of defense in the event of an overspeed event. It is CRUCIAL that the valve discs align to the valve seats to have proper sealing. The unit can overspeed with only 3% of steam with no load on the generator. A catastrophic event is possible if the TTV were to fail and the V1 control valves did not seal. During the next outage it is recommended to machine the steam chest at the stem bushing and seat fits so that the fits are round and concentric to one another. Stem bushings and seats with stock should be ordered. The stem bushing with stock part number is PN# 101C459CA-101 (QTY5). The seat drawing does not have a part number that has extra stock. The original seat drawing is B709C06B. Five (5) new seats should be ordered and the manufacturer contacted to add 0.125” at the “A” dimension (2 locations, upper and lower). If the manufacturer can not meet the request, an Engineering ER case should be opened for a weld procedure. The seats should be welded and machined down to 4.375” at the “A” dimension. The seats and welding (if needed) should be procured/fabricated well in advance of the outage. CBM: NA

Part Condition: Good Part Description: The turbine rotor disassembled and put on the rotor stands that customer has provided. A visual inspection has been carried out and ER case ER-20191204-0537 opened for findings. The critical findings were the indication seen on a blade near the notch at stage 14, heavy rubbing and material build up on the blade covers at the first 6 stages. To be sure of the indication an stage 14 blade, red dye inspection done on the indication and confirmed that the indication was a crack. During this time, transportation skid was modified per the turbine rotor dimensions. After that, the DSW Rotor (SN# X1352333) was shipped to the NIDCO facility for blast clean and NDT. All blasting occurred outside of the NIDCO facility and while the rotor was still in the shipping stands. It should be noted that this made it difficult to perform a thorough A/O cleaning, as did the turbine competency of the cleaners. After the rotor was A/O blast cleaned, magnetic particle inspection was performed on the rotor surface. A crack at the 14th stage special blade (next to the notch) was observed. This crack was also visually found during disassembly of the rotor. During further inspection, some surface indications on the 14th stage wheel were found where the notch is cut into the wheel. The indications were lightly polished and removed as it was determined to be a fab line from making the wheel notch or installing the blades. The 14th stage blade indication was evaluated by Engineering under ER Case ER-20191211-0177. The final resolution implemented was to cut the blade just under the area of indication. GE OSS was mobilized to the NIDCO facility to execute this work. The blade and cover were removed with caution to remove minimal material and to save all material removed. The material removed was weighed after removal and totaled 263.5 grams. NDT was conducted after the blade was lightly profiled to remove any sharp edges or upset material. No indications were found. Built up metal material was noted in several areas of the rotor. This material was from spill strip damaged caused by a reported loss of oil and bearing wiping event. The amount of material ranged from stage to stage. The most severe areas were the 2nd and 6th stage that are shown in the accompanied pictures. The metal build-up was hand dressed by GE OSS while still onsite. Rotor Low Speed Balancing (LSB) commenced on approximately January 5th, 2020. IMHP provided the LSB skid to the NIDCO facility. A subcontractor was utilized to record and analyze the unbalance data. A separate GE OSS bucket/balance technician was mobilized to site for direction and staking of the balance weights. The LSB process proved difficult for several reasons including, but not limited to; balancing format between GE and subcontractor, balancing procedure between GE and subcontractor, direction from Engineering, time zone barriers, and an assortment of where and how data was collected and communicated on all ends. It is recommended to open the Engineering Requisitions well prior to the actual balancing to open a line of communication with engineering and potentially shift work schedules to ease transmission of information. The rotor LSB was complete Jan-10, 2020 @ 0600. The final unbalance on the rotor was left at 0.04mm/s @ 97 deg on Bearing #1 and 0.05 mm/s @ 322 deg on Bearing #2. After the rotor balancing was complete, the balance end weights and set screws were staked. After receiving the rotor from NIDCO, the nozzle box and the stub shaft installed in place using SKF hydraulic tool. Then the rotor installed in place, the axial and radial runouts measured for the stub shaft. Also, NDT carried out for the balance weight staked areas and no indication observed. Rotor journal areas had small circumferential scratches coming from the event in 2011. These areas cleaned with fine emery cloth paper

. Rotor journal areas had small circumferential scratches coming from the event in 2011. These areas cleaned with fine emery cloth paper. Keep in mind that, this scratches will have no impact on the operation of the turbine since they are circumferential. The coupling and the thrust collar surfaces was found in good condition, no problem seen. Recommendation Status: Should be planned for next Outage Recommendation Type: Repairs Recommendation Description: Customer should order the parts for the repair of the cut blade including the notch, pin, reamers, two covers and the other next blade to the notch if repair work will be done. (ER case need to be opened for this subject. ) Also, during the next major outage inspection, mobilization of an experienced crew of Aluminum Oxide Sandblasters either to the DSW site or to an offsite facility for cleaning is needed. Power rollers or an alternative means of rotating the rotor should be available for blasting and NDT to ensure a thorough cleaning and inspection. Resources were challenging to get into the region during this outage. A skilled bucket tech to do clean and dress on the blade partitions was not available. It is recommended next outage to have a GE OSS bucket technician available that is familiar with the process to do clean and dress on the blades next outage, particularly in the 2nd thru 6th stages. The low speed balancing (LSB) process proved difficult for several reasons including, but not limited to; balancing format between GE and subcontractor, balancing procedure between GE and subcontractor, direction from Engineering, time zone barriers, and an assortment of where and how data was collected and communicated on all ends. It is recommended to open the Engineering Requisitions well prior to the actual balancing to open a line of communication with engineering and potentially shift work schedules to ease transmission of information. The vendor recording data should also be screened prior to the outage to ensure the data recording will be performed per GE Specifications. If the customer requires the rotor journal surfaces to be machined, then a ER case need to be opened and new bearings are required with the stock material on the Babbitt surfaces. Part Condition: Good Part Description: First, 3 inch pipe on the right side of the casing was cut out to remove the upper half (UH) turbine casing. Then the turbine casing removed and placed in the turbine hall while the on shell mounted valve (V1 gear valve) was still assembled. After removing the gear valve, UH turbine casing transferred to the old turbine building and being flipped over. Then, the UH and LH diaphragms and packing casings removed. On the lower half (LH) casing and UH casing, NDT (red dye) has been carried out on horizontal joint and most of the diaphragm grooves after cleaning the casings. No indication observed during the NDT tests. Besides, the UH and LH inner casing has been blast cleaned and NDT inspected during the outage and no indication observed. The NDT reports for the casings is attached to the Appendix section of this report. Also, during the TOPS ON / TOPS OFF alignment checks the contact of both casing has been checked at horizontal joint while every second bolt has been tightened by hammering until the gap closed. Contact was good on most of the surface. After the TOPS ON/TOPS OFF alignment and NDT of the main parts such as rotor, diaphragms etc. The parts installed in places. After that, upper half casing installed, and all bolts are torqued per GE specs such as stretching by angle or with a torque value. (Extension inspection sheet attached.) After the torquing, sound test showed no loosen studs. Also, gap check has been done on the final close, did not show any problem. During the visual check no problem seen on the rupture disc as well. Recommendation Status: Should be planned for next Outage Recommendation Type: Services Recommendation Description: The bolt heaters that were used during the outage was not the original one. Also, there was heating problem with the bolt heaters used. Therefore, customer should test the bolt heaters on their hand and investigate what is the problem with the bolt heaters or order 3-4 new bolt heaters from GE. Full set of studs, nuts, bolts and pins should be ordered for the next outage. Also, consumables should be ordered for the next outage such as Birkosit, Alinco, Molykote, RTV

Part Condition: Good Part Description: The nozzle box was removed from the casing together with the turbine rotor. Special tooling (bearing assembly) was used to position the nozzle box on the rotor. After removal of the stub shaft (coupling) and rotor gear ring, the nozzle box was rigged and removed from the rotor. The nozzle box was sent to NIDCO workshop for cleaning and inspection. Aluminum oxide blast cleaning was performed on all critical area, followed by visual and NDT inspections. Visual inspection revealed a good condition of the whole nozzle box assembly, except the spill strip that was found damaged at the lower/bottom side. Decision was made to remove the upset material and reuse the spill strip as is. Replacement of the spill strip would be time consuming and requires new parts and machining preparation. It may be scheduled for replacement during a future major outage. NDT inspection revealed a good condition of the nozzle box assembly as well, except an indication found on the weld of the upper access plug. The indication was removed by light grinding/blending and. the area was NDT retested. The valve seat sealing rings were found stuck and could not be moved due to the oxide deposits. Decision was made to replace the seal ring assemblies with new parts. The old parts were removed, the seal ring bores were cleaned, and the new ring assemblies were measured, fitted and locked per specification. Extensive cleaning was performed inside the nozzle box prior and after sealing rings installation. The nozzle box was installed first in the casing for alignment purpose. The lower half packing housing was installed and dowelled in place, and the nozzle box was installed in the casing on the original shims for the alignment readings. Finally, the nozzle box was installed on the rotor then inside the casing together with the rotor. The original support shims were reused, no additional machining was required as the alignment was found within acceptable limits. New bolting hardware was installed at both horizontal joint and vertical joint with proper gap and/or torque tightening. All bolting was locked per design. New N1G6 packing ring was installed, however the original packing ring was installed at N1G5 location due to the lack of spare new part. Before V1 vale installation, the nozzle box sealing rings were lubricated and aligned by using a special alignment tool fabricated at customer’s machine shop. Recommendation Status: Should be planned for next Outage Recommendation Type: Repairs Recommendation Description: Replacement of the damaged nozzle box spill strips should be planned for the next major outage when the machine is opened. All parts should be ordered in advance and replacement procedure and schedule should be agreed with the selected vendor. Part Condition: Fair Part Description: After removal from the casings, all diaphragms were sent to NIDCO workshop for cleaning and inspection. Aluminum oxide blast cleaning was performed on all critical area, followed by visual and NDT inspections. Most of the diaphragm nozzle/partitions were found in good condition and appropriate for further service. Several exceptions were noted and are documented below: Light to medium partition damage was noticed on Stage #3 and Stage #4 diaphragm partitions. The noticed damages consisted of pipping like indications, and bending of the partition trailing edges, possibly FOD. Repair options were discussed with GE Engineering, documented by ER-20200107-0461. The final decision was made to cut back the trailing edges up to 1/8” and reprofile the partition in order to correct the partition surface and to restore the trailing edges thickness per drawing. All these repairs were performed by GE certified diaphragm technicians. NDT (LP) was performed on all partitions after repair and no indication was reported. An indication was detected on one partition of Stage #11 U/H diaphragm. The indication was removed by grinding and the partition was restored by welding and hand machining. The repair was performed by GE certified diaphragm technician. NDT (LP) was performed after repair and no indication was present. Two partitions were found damaged/bent, one on each Stage #17 Upper half Diaphragm and Lower half diaphragm respectively, both located at the HJ area. It is assumed that the damages occurred during transportation and handling. Both partitions were straightened, weld repaired and restored by GE certified technicians. NDT (LP) was performed after repairs and no indication was reported. Inspection of the other diaphragm components (diaphragm webs, rings, horizontal joints, keys, dowels, support lag assemblies, set screws etc.) did not reveal major issues, except the conditions documented below: An indication was reported following NDT inspection of the Stage #3 diaphragm, located on the diaphragm web, exit side, running from the packing drain hole down to the partitions. Further investigation revealed that the reported indication was a light erosion trace. It was removed by light polishing and NDT (LP) re-tested. Finally, the component was released for service. Significant damage was found at all diaphragm spill strips, bottom side. The damage was most probably related to the loss of bearing supply oil and bearing failure event experienced in 2011. At that time the bearing babbitt was partially wiped out due to the shaft rotation without oil, leading to a rotor drop that damaged the spill strips at the bottom side. This damage was noticed on all stages from #2 to #16 (stages #17 and #18 are different design). Different scenarios were discussed with customer i.e. replacement or repair of the spill strips during the outage. Considering the lack of parts and extensive time required to replace the spill strips, it was decided to repair the damaged spill strip areas. All upset material was removed, and the spill strips were reshaped, making sure that no material may get loose and release later into the steam path. Diaphragm axial crush pins and casing diaphragm slots were measured, and the amount of pins adjustment was determined. Slight adjustment of some of the axial crush pins was required in order to achieve the desired clearance: stages #5, #6, #8, #9, #10, #15, #16, and #17. Adjustment of the crush pins was performed by welding with Inconel followed by manual grinding/filing. Welding was performed by GE certified diaphragm technicians. At reassembly, the L/H diaphragms side slip was adjusted as well and brought within the specified tolerances. This was performed by diaphragm centering slots welding, followed by manual grinding/filing. Welding was performed by GE certified diaphragm technicians. Side slip adjustment was required for the stages: #2, #3, #9, #14, #15, #16, #17 and #18

. Welding was performed by GE certified diaphragm technicians. Side slip adjustment was required for the stages: #2, #3, #9, #14, #15, #16, #17 and #18. All diaphragm installation hardware (set screws, lugs, etc.) as well as all packing rings & springs were replaced with new parts. Lower half diaphragms were aligned first by laser, considering the Tops Off / Tops On bore moves; the final alignment was done by using one electronic alignment tool (ERAG/CAT) provided by GE tool center. The corresponding upper half diaphragms were leveled based on lower half diaphragms alignment. Recommendation Status: Should be planned for next Outage Recommendation Type: Repairs Recommendation Description: Replacement of the damaged diaphragm spill strips should be planned for the next major outage when the machine is opened. All parts should be ordered in advance and replacement procedure and schedule should be agreed with the selected vendor

Part Condition: Good Part Description: The Trip Throttle Valve (TTV) was removed and shipped to NIDCO for disassembly, cleaning, inspection, any repairs, parts replacement, and reassembly during this outage. Prior to GE/ FieldCore arrival to the NIDCO shop, the valve upper head “bonnet” was removed and the Pressure Seal Head (PSH) pull down ring disassembled. It was reported that the upper head nuts were not easily disassembled. The use of hydraulic wrenches in combination with heating the nuts with a torch was needed to remove the nuts. One (1) stud was cut during disassembly, which was not advised by GE/FieldCore. After the TTV upper head was removed, the TTV casing was stood upright and the TTV assembly removed. The TTV assembly looked to generally be in good condition. No steam erosion, visual cracks, or signs of stressing or overheating were visually observed. A small gall in the TTV casing at the PSH fit was noted but looked to be old damage. Dimensional checks were conducted on the old TTV assembly to have some type of baseline as the dimensional data is not available from the Gimpel OEM manufacturer. All dimensional inspections can be found on the accompanied data sheets. The TTV casing was Aluminum Oxide grit blast cleaned during this outage. The flanges welds, valve seat welds, anti-swirl dam, and gasketed surfaces were all blast cleaned then dye penetrant tested (PT). Porosity was found on the small flange welds in several areas. One (1) small indication was also found on a leak-off flange. It was determined that the indication was undercutting from the toe of the weld pass above it. The steam dam had several areas of porosity noted. The valve seat was PT tested with no indications reported. The upper head studs were cleaned and Ultrasonically Tested (UT). No indications were noted. The TTV assembly was assembled with all new parts with the exception of the main disc valve cap. A new valve stem, PSH, PSH backseat, split rings, pilot valve, pilot valve cap, and valve cap pin were used. The pilot valve cap and main disc valve cap bolts only came with one (1) bolt each. The most damaged bolt on each cap was removed from service and replaced new. For All critical dimensions were rechecked and recorded on the accompanied data sheets. There were some areas that were found to be different between the two (2) assemblies, but nothing that appeared to be compromising to the operation of the valve. The pilot valve was assembled with a new gasket during reassembly. There was a small gap under the cap after the bolting was final torqued, but it is unknown if that is by design. The pilot lift check was notably different from the assembly removed from service and the new assembly. Contact checks were conducted on the TTV assembly between the valve stem and backseat as well as between the valve main disc internal seat and the pilot valve. Both areas were found to be 100% contact with no lapping required. The TTV casing was thoroughly cleaned prior to the installation of the new TTV assembly. The TTV assembly was installed and the main disc-to-seat contact checked. The contact was found to be 100% with no lapping required, which is not typical for a unit in operation. The TTV assembly was then final installed with a new gasket. New pulldown rings were used to assemble the PSH after the valve was installed. The as found bolting was reused and tightened until the PSH gasket was crushed. The jam nuts were then tightened to lock the ring in place. The TTV upper head was not reassembled at the NIDCO facility. TTV Studs: One (1) TTV stud was cut during disassembly of the upper head. Another stud was found backed out and determined to need removal, as the stud engagement was less than one times the diameter of the stud. To prevent damage to the bolt hole, the stud was cut off at the joint and drilled out with the other stud that was cut. Both bolt holes were tapped by a tap supplied by NIDCO after the stud shanks were removed

. Both bolt holes were tapped by a tap supplied by NIDCO after the stud shanks were removed. New studs were not available while the valve was at NIDCO so therefore not installed at the shop. Two (2) small studs (Part 108 on TTV OEM Drawing NP-2312) were broken during disassembly. These studs are the studs that are on top of the upper head. It’s unclear to the writer why the flange was removed at all. The studs were drilled out of the upper head by NIDCO. New studs were made from bolting that was cut from the TTV upper head studs. The original studs were then misplaced and two (2) more studs made from an old casing bolt. The studs were installed after the valve was shipped back to site. TTV Steam Strainer: The TTV steam strainer was blast cleaned and NDT’d during this outage. The strainer looked to be in good condition. A few of the screen holes were found to be oversized from presumably a previous repair or removal of debris. The holes were left as-is during this outage but are recommended to be planned for plugging during the next outage. During the TTV steam strainer NDT small indications were found at the welds securing the strainer to the upper head. There were a total of eleven (11) indications. The indications were ground by NIDCO under the direction of FieldCore. Previous Engineering Case ER-20160217-1896 was used as a guide during the repair, as this valve was provided by Gimpel under the same GE specification drawing. The rod selected in the case (E16-8-2) was not readily available in Israel. For this reason, a substitute Inconel rod was used per other similar PAC case. All welds were NDT’d after welding complete with no indications noted. TTV Hydraulics: Hydraulic actuator was separated from valve chest since valve had to be shipped in NIDCO premises; Actuator was disassembled for inspection, cleaning, new parts replacement and reassembly. Springs’ seating surface on piston was found extremely dirty, partially covered in sludge (probably caused by moisture condensation). Hydraulic actuator cylinder’s inner surface and piston (guide side skirt surface) were noted with slight score marks, cleaned with finest oiled emery cloth and ScotchBrite. Relay valve was disassembled from actuator cylinder, cleaned and fitted with new o- rings. New parts replaced: - Piston ring (only one of two was available and replaced) - Relay piston ring - Spindle roller bearing - Round paper gaskets (2x) for gear housing and square Garlock gasket for relay valve cover. - O-rings to relay valve and solenoid trip valve. During the cold commisioning checks, TTV tested with trip signals, however did not open after the trips. After that, to check the reason, relay valve removed and cleaned. Also, the distance between hydralic actuator stem and valve stem set to 0.131" (was found as 0.529"). Recommendation Status: Should be planned for next Outage Recommendation Type: Repairs Recommendation Description: Little information is available on the Gimpel valves. It is recommended that the OEM be consulted prior to the next outage for critical dimensional data if the valve assembly is to be reused and to have a baseline for new parts as it is the writer’s opinion that new parts should also be inspected as a quality best practice. The TTV steam strainer was found with a few perforations (holes) that were oversized at some point. GE DWG# 165A974BE specifies that these perforations be no larger than 3/16”. It is recommended that prior to the next outage the GE team submit an ER case to engineering with direction on how to repair the holes. The specification outlines that the strainer should be made of 300 series SS, preferably 304 or 316. The site team should inquire to engineering for recommendations if the screen can be directly welded or pins should be fabricated and sized to each enlarged hole specifically. The GE team should also inquire what welding rod can be used that would be compatible for all 300 series stainless steel

. The GE team should also inquire what welding rod can be used that would be compatible for all 300 series stainless steel. Valve piston score marks are recommended to be monitored. Before next steam turbine’s inspection, a visual inspection is suggested through cover disassembly and relay valve removal to provide borescope access. If score marks are worse than as found during current outage, OEM Gimpel Corporation shall be consulted for further action and possible new piston replacement. Besides, full set of studs, nuts and multiple gaskets for connecting flanges should be ordered for the next outage. Customer should also keep a full set of valve cover studs, nuts and gaskets for the next outage. chunk_text: Part Condition: Fair Part Description: V1 Valve Gear: The V1 valve gear was disassembled, cleaned, inspected, repaired, parts exchanged, and reassembled at the NIDCO facility during this outage. After the valve was disassembled the steam chest was aluminum oxide blast cleaned and NDT’d. The results of the NDT section are discussed in the “Steam Chest” section below. All areas of the V1 valve gear assembly were inspected and can be summarized in their respective sections below. The most severe finding were the bushing and seat bores. It is recommended next outage to re-bore these areas and install oversized seats and bushings. After the new parts were installed, cleaned, measured, etc., the V1 valve gear was reassembled at the NIDCO facility. All parts that were provided from the customer stock order prior to the outage were used. Two (2) of the new valve bushings per PN# 101C459CA-1 that were allocated to the #3 and #4 V1 CVs were found with insufficient internal diameters. The stems could not be freely inserted into the bushings. Other than this issue no major issues were encountered when reassembling the V1 control valve. Steam Chest: The V1 control valve steam chest was NDT’d after completion of the A/O blast cleaning. Two (2) indications were found during the inspection. One (1) small indication was found at the #3 valve seat flange location. The indication was found at the gasket sealing area. ER Case 20191226-0131 was generated for engineering disposition. The indication was left as-is. This is largely due to the location of the indication. It is recommended to monitor the indication during the next outage inspection. The second indication was found internal to the steam chest. This indication has likely been in the casing for several years of operation. The crack does exceed the criteria for no action outlined in EM 2502. However, due to the location of the crack it was left as is. Both indications should be monitored next outage. If the indications propagate, they should be removed, and engineering consulted to evaluate if the indications need repaired after excavation. The V1 control valve steam chest was thoroughly cleaned prior to reassembly. All flange surfaces were cleaned and stoned. All bolt/nut spot faces were cleaned and polished to remove any upset metal from previous bolting cycles. Camshaft: The V1 camshaft was cleaned and dimensionally inspected after disassembly. All shaft surfaces corresponding to the DU bearing locations were PT tested. No indications were found. The shaft was also UT inspected. During the UT inspection an indication was found (measuring from either end) near the pinion gear. No action was taken this outage. A spare camshaft should be ordered and available for the next valve outage. The Customer should plan to remove the pinion and perform UT in the radial direction to access the indication. If the indication is found during the extended inspection, the shaft should be replaced. New shaft keys for the cams and pinion should also be available during this inspection. Camshaft runout was inspected and found to be satisfactory. The TIR was found to be; 0.002" @ #1, 0.000" @ #2, 0.002" @ #3, 0.004" @ #4, and 0.006" @ #5. The camshaft was installed with the DU bearings to expand the bearings as several were found distorted. After the bearings were expanded the IDs were dimensionally inspected. Several were found "tight" but suitable for operation. Camshaft Bearing Blocks: The #3 and #4 Camshaft bearing blocks were removed to facilitate the removal of the stem bushings. The #3 bearing block was found with multiple shims under the block, mostly on the aft side of the block. The #4 bearing block was found with no shims. The bearing blocks were reinstalled with shims and a levelness check conducted. The check showed that the #3 block was sitting very high. For this reason, the shims were removed, and the levelness check started with no shims

After the camshaft bearing blocks were leveled, the bearing block caps were installed. The #1 and #5 blocks were originally found with shims. The shims were cleaned and reinstalled but found to make the #5 ID of the block much larger than the design specifications outlined on GE DWG 128C129BF, Zone C-5. All final camshaft bearing block IDs are provided on form D310205. The blocks have an area that does not meet he mentioned design specifications. However, the camshaft was installed and moved freely in each area. It’s recommended that next outage the blocks be re-inspected. If the IDs continue to increase, then the block joints should be machined or the blocks replaced. The new camshaft bearing block liners were installed into the bearing blocks after the blocks were cleaned and measured. The liners were found to be oddly shaped and not conform to the blocks. The cam shaft was then installed to expand the liners. The camshaft was then removed, and the liners measured. Camshaft Rollers: The camshaft rollers and camshaft roller bushings were replaced new during this outage. For this reason, dimensional measurements were not recorded. No issues with fitting the pins at final assembly were encountered and all rollers moved freely during the initial stroking of the V1 valve. Lever Arms: The V1 control valve linkage arms were disassembled, cleaned, and inspected while at the NIDCO facility. The old pins were not measured in the interest of time. The new pin dimensions were input based on the design value to save time on measuring when inspecting the clearance between the linkage pins and the arms. The design clearance is 0.001" to 0.003". For this reason, anything 0.007" and over was flagged. Any area from 0.007" to 0.009" should be monitored and prepared for repair next outage. Any area 0.010" and over was flagged as red to be repaired this outage. · Install insert (1.502” OD x 1.250” ID) at CV #2 Left Lever arm at “A” location · Install insert (1.502” OD x 1.250” ID) at CV #2 Right Lever arm at “C” location · Install insert (1.502” OD x 1.250” ID) at CV #4 Right Lever arm at “C” location NIDCO facility manufactured the inserts and installed onsite. The inserts were all made to be 0.002” press fit to the arms. The inserts were staked into place to secure them for future disassembly cycles. No issues were reported when installing the inserts and all pins fit nicely during reassembly. Stem Link: The stem link bearings and pins were replaced during this outage. As found dimensional checks were not recorded to save time and resources during the outage. All bearings were pressed out at the NIDCO shop. chunk_text: . In both areas, on all valves, the holes were worn elliptical and oversized. The stem bushing fits ranged from 0.002” to 0.009” (100% to 400%) oversized. The seat fits ranged from 0.013” to .041” (500% to 1,200%) oversized and severely out of round. It is not uncommon to see the stem chest seat and bushings to be oversized and distorted on a unit in service. To fix the issue, the stem bushing bore is minimally resized to be round. The seat bore is then skim cut to be round while holding 0.004” concentricity to the stem bushing bore. This could have been completed in the NIDCO facility. However, this requires oversized stem bushing and seat parts which were not available. The bushings and seats were assembled as best possible. When the seats were installed, two (2) indicators were set up on the seat on an “X” and “Y” axis. The bolting was tightened until the gasket was just about to crush. The seat was then pushed to the extreme on each side of the “X” and “Y”, then pushed to the opposite side. The seat was then centered between the two values on both axes. The valves were then “slammed” shut as to self-align the valves to the seats. The bolting was then torqued per GE specification with indicators monitoring movement as the bolting was tightened. The V1 valve is the first line of defense in the event of an overspeed event. It is CRUCIAL that the valve discs align to the valve seats to have proper sealing. The unit can overspeed with only 3% of steam with no load on the generator. A catastrophic event is possible if the TTV were to fail and the V1 control valves did not seal. During the next outage it is recommended to machine the steam chest at the stem bushing and seat fits so that the fits are round and concentric to one another. Stem bushings and seats with stock should be ordered. The stem bushing with stock part number is PN# 101C459CA-101 (QTY5). The seat drawing does not have a part number that has extra stock. The original seat drawing is B709C06B. Five (5) new seats should be ordered and the manufacturer contacted to add 0.125” at the “A” dimension (2 locations, upper and lower). If the manufacturer can not meet the request, an Engineering ER case should be opened for a weld procedure. The seats should be welded and machined down to 4.375” at the “A” dimension. The seats and welding (if needed) should be procured/fabricated well in advance of the outage. Recommendation Status: Should be planned for next Outage Recommendation Type: Repairs Recommendation Description: Scheduled valve outages are an essential part of the steam turbines life cycle and maintenance program. The valves have several functions, including preventing to the unit from an overspeed event. GE recommends having valve outages between major outage inspections. The valve outages are typically in 3-5 year intervals. More information on the valve outage recommendations can be found in the GE instruction manual that includes the applicable GEK/GEI’s. Recommendations for the V1 Control specifically can be found in GE Document EM1953 and GEK72354. It is recommended that DSW establish an effective maintenance program that supports the mentioned documentation and outage cycles. Overall the selection of consumable spare parts was good. The only issues encountered on minor parts were lock tabs for the pillow blocks and caps. Add PN#s 101A783AB-2 (QTY 20) & 101A639AB-23 (QTY 10) to the list when ordering the hardware for the valves. There were also some nuts for the dowels missing. Order PN# N245BP29 (QTY 20) as with the lock tabs. The stem clevis bolts could also be replaced. Add PN# 8954949AA-21 (QTY 10) as well. chunk_text: Part Condition: Good Part Description: Flow to #5 steam extraction is controlled through a high-pressure oil hydraulically operated shell mounted axial flow grid type valve. Valve assembly consists of a multi-ported split ring that once rotated allows and controls steam flow through a respective, adjoining multi-ported split stationary diaphragm. Ring rotation is achieved through yoke- clevis-pivot block engagement, contrary to older versions that had a rack and gear configuration. Valve cover and mounted actuator were disassembled from turbine’s upper half casing. Upon turbine’s upper half shell disassembly and lift, grid valve was found in very good condition, able to slide easily by hand, without much effort. V2 valve; assembly and cover: Valve’s upper and lower half rings and diaphragms were split and disassembled/ lifted from turbine to facilitate rotor’s removal. All four parts were shipped to NIDCO premises for aluminum oxide blasting and NDTs inspection and assessment. Valve cover was sent later to NIDCO for machining, as new parts had been delivered oversized (upper guide, guide plate, front & rear guides) and had to be precision planned to design dimensions in order to obtain new rod alignment/ smooth slide and wear-free operation of the mechanism/ correct clearances at the slide/ proper and sealed reassembly. However, old guide plate reinstalled to keep the design dimensions. Since planning were correctly executed as asked from NIDCO, guides’ underside added shims found during disassembly (had been installed in 2011 outage to compensate) were not re-installed. Valve’s rings and diaphragms were visually and MPI inspected after sand blasting, without findings. Bolting hardware (split joint) was replaced with new in the assembly and the valve cover (dowels, guide pins and screws). Internal parts of valve’s cover were replaced with new, namely: - All guides - Valve’s rod and its spherical bearing/ snap ring, clevis, block-pivot and its pins, - Valve’s rod coupling (adapter), guide bushing, retainer flange and screws V2 Extraction grid valve; Operating Cylinder (actuator) Miller high-pressure hydraulic actuator was separated from valve cover and disassembled for inspection, cleaning, new parts replacement and reassembly. Pilot valve’s, cylinder’s and parts’ general condition was acceptable, cylinder’s dimensions and stem run-out was recorded, new o-rings were installed, and a new MOOG solenoid valve was installed with new o- rings in oil ports. Actuator was also fitted with a new LVDT positioner and rod spherical bearing, available on-site. Actuator’s stem was also fitted with a new rod coupling (adapter) manufactured in NIDCO from 1.7225 (42CrMo4) steel as per GE’s manufacturing drawing recommendation. Valve’s and actuator’s rods’ coupling halves are identical and bear same part number (3122J86P002). Recommendation Status: Should be planned for next Outage Recommendation Type: Parts Recommendation Description: The grid valve needs to be inspected in the next planned outage as the scope of minor inspection. The customer should order spares for the minor inspection. Actuator condition is exceptional but as a good maintenance practice, power plant is recommended to source Miller hydraulic actuator repair kit (wiper, seals, o- rings for the piston) that can be stored and used in case of emergency. Part Condition: Poor Part Description: Steam turbine was equipped with two 20’’ x 24’’ spring loaded safety valves. The indications were ground out of the ears and the ears welded back with a NIDCO provided welding rod for cast steels. Upon parts’ return from NIDCO, valve was reassembled per as found values according OEM procedure. chunk_text: Part Condition: Fair Part Description: For supplying low pressure steam for fertilizers’ plant’s processes Unit is equipped with 2x 10’’ flanged uncontrolled non-return valves (#1 & #3, 8,5 bar), 2x 12’’ flanged uncontrolled non-return valves (#2 & #4, 4,5 bar) and 1x 42’’ controlled non-return valve (#5, body welded in the steam pipe). Installed valves had been manufactured by Atwood & Morrill and are all of free-flow, reverse current type valves. As per Customer’s Operations’ department remarks, installed check valves were not operating properly; Probably due to pneumatic actuators stuck thus preventing disks to return in ‘’closed’’ position when air was supplied (forced to close). Depending on steam supply to BOP processes and steam piping Customer’s works, all four flanged check valves were removed from piping and shipped in NIDCO premises for disassembly, aluminum oxide blasting, NDTs, inspection, new parts replacement, disk blue contact check, reassembly and replacement to process steam 10 & 12’’ piping. Upon first 10 &12’’ valves’ parts return from NIDCO (batch ‘’a’’), valves were reassembled on-site using all new internal parts (shafts, bushings, spacers, set screws, dog bones), new graphite packing rings, bolting hardware and gaskets. Second set of 10 &12’’ valves (b) was re-assembled in NIDCO machine shop with all new parts available (as replaced in first ‘’a’’ batch) and Prussian blue contact check were performed before final assembly. All as-found pneumatic actuators, solenoid valves (Asco RedHat) and position limit switches were replaced with new. New stainless-steel supports manufactured from Customer to install new actuators and their limit switches on #1 to #4 check valves (10 & 12’’) as corrosion had destroyed the old ones. Recommendation Status: Should be planned for next Outage Recommendation Type: Operations Recommendation Description: New limit switches and pneumatic actuators shall be protected from condensate spills that may corrode their moving parts and stems, providing wrong indications to turbine’s control system or result in NRV malfunction (fail to close when necessary on Unit’s trip). Also, seeing the condition of the check valves after the previous major inspection in this outage, we recommend that customer should plan to change all the 10" and 12" extraction valves with new ones in the next outage CBM: NA AS FOUND CONDITION OF ACTUATOR 10?? chunk_text: Extraction valve cover was removed, no difficulty was encountered removing the cover nuts and cover. The valve lever arm assemblies and weights were removed from both the air cylinder and non-cylinder side. Difficulty was encountered with disassembly due to size constraints. A note should be made that the setscrews in the shaft arm are difficult to disassemble due to them being peened. Valve stem was also difficult to remove, it should be made aware that the disc/disc arm assembly should be properly supported to facilitate removal of shaft and internals. Both the air cylinder and non-cylinder mechanical seals were removed, then the shaft was removed along with 2 sets of bushings and spacers. The disc/disc arm assembly was removed and shipped to third party vendor Nidco, for disassembly, sand blasting and reassembly. The following valve internal parts were replaced with new this outage: shaft, mechanical seals, spacer and bushings. Once disc/disc arm assembly returned from Nidco, valve reassembly commenced. No difficulties were encountered during re-installation of valve internals. Valve disc seating was verified using feeler gauges. Valve counterweights were reinstalled along with a new air cylinder and limit switches. Valve cover was reinstalled with new gasket. No difficulties were encountered during installation of valve cover.

chunk_text: Part Condition: Fair Part Description: The combined lubrication and control oil system was inspected during this outage. This included the disassembly, inspection and reassembly of the AC lube oil pumps, DC lube oil pump, vapor extractor and Lube Oil Coolers. Hydraulic pumps were replaced with new this outage. DC lube oil pump was removed from the lube oil tank then disassembled and inspected. During ball bearing disassembly, a step was found on the pump shaft. Due to not having a replacement shaft onsite, ICL spare pump was used. Spare pump was disassembled and inspected. New ball bearings were installed. Dimensional checks were performed on the impeller, impeller casing and shaft. All dimensional checks were within tolerance and required no further action. Spare DC lube oil pump was reassembled without incident. Pump was installed in the lube oil tank with new gaskets. AC lube oil pumps were removed from the lube oil tank, then disassembled and inspected. Pump motors were removed and given to ICL for shipment to third party vendor for refurbishment. No significant or unusual problems were noted during lube oil pump disassembly. Dimensional checks were performed on the impeller, impeller casing and shaft. All dimensional checks were within tolerance and required no further action. During this overhaul, ball bearings and oil seals were supplied by ICL and replaced. Associated discharge check valves were removed and visually inspected. Inspections revealed no deficiencies and were reinstalled with new gaskets. Both AC lube oil pumps have discharge butterfly valves. Vales were found with damaged rubber sealing surfaces. New butterfly valves were obtained from ICL and reinstalled. Hydraulic pumps were removed from the lube oil tank then sent to the ICL shop for storage. Hydraulic pump motors were given to ICL for shipment to third party vendor for refurbishment. ICL supplied new hydraulic pumps. One pump was brand new and the second was refurbished from a previous outage. Visual inspections were performed on the new pumps, and no deficiencies were noted. Pumps were checked to ensure that they were filled with oil prior to installation. Motors arrived back on site and were reinstalled on the lube oil tank without incident. New couplings were supplied by ICL and installed on hydraulic pumps and motors. Accumulators underwent inspection and pre-charge was checked. Pre-charge was found to be less than 55.2 +/- 1.7 Bar per GEK 104154. Nitrogen accumulators were recharged and were found to be holding pressure at 54 Bar. Lube Oil Coolers were inspected during this outage. Flanges on the inlet and outlet water piping were removed and the lube oil coolers were inspected. Visual inspection revealed no deficiencies. Customer elected to remove cooler covers and water piping to perform a leak check on the coolers. Leak check revealed no leaks in the cooler and no other issues were noted. Lube oil cooler covers, and piping was reinstalled with new gaskets. Vapor extractor was removed from the lube oil tank and disassembled. No deficiencies were noted during visual inspection of the motor and vapor extractor assembly. Motor was given to ICL for shipment to third party vendor for refurbishment. Once motor arrived back on site, vapor extractor was reassembled without incident. Recommendation Status: Should be planned for next Outage Recommendation Type: Parts Recommendation Description: Correct spare parts should be ordered for the next outage. Also, the cleanness and the condition of the lube oil and the lube oil system should be monitored during operations. chunk_text: Part Description: Turbine to Generator alignment checked prior to turbine disassembly. However, it was observed that the generator did not lift with the lifting oil. ER case ER-20191127-0902 was opened and the alignment was found to be out of tolerance as given in drawing 165A753EA Field Alignment Data. Scaffolding was erected around the Generator foundations, holding down bolts released and the area including generator base-plate feet, center keys cleaned. Hydraulic jacks, plates and shims prepared for generator movements. Alignment changes were calculated, and shims changes are done per calculations. After that generator moved sideways per the calculations. The as left final data was measured within tolerance. The Generator holding down bolts were adjusted for 0.010” clearance and locking tabs tack welded in place. Recommendation Status: Should be planned for next Outage Recommendation Description: Customer should keep the plates, shims, hydraulic jacks and other equipment in clean and working condition for the next outage. I strongly advice to prepare proper plates or shims to be used with hydraulic jacks for the next outage. chunk_text: Part Description: General Electric performed on this generator a major outage as suggested by GEK103566 adding the field extraction after the Magic inspection performed in 2017 where it was find a large area of loose wedges. This generator has worked between 1-1-2015 to 29-11-2019 for 41130 hour, around 8300 hours/year close to a load of 20 MW . Recommendation Description: See the attached file with the control checks , pictures and conclusions.

3 1. Introduction General Electric performed on this generator a major outage as suggested by GEK103566 adding the field extraction after the Magic inspection performed in 2017 where it was find a large area of loose wedges. This generator has worked between 1-1-2015 to 29-11-2019 for 41130 hour, around 8300 hours/year close to a load of 20 MW . The following main actions performed:  Loto on the Generator and steam turbine  Disassembling of the acoustic cabinet  Opening of the coupling  Opening of the stator;  Field extraction;  Electrical Tests: o Insulation resistance & PI on the field and the exciter; o Copper resistance of the generator field and exciter field and armature; o Impedance of the generator field; o Copper resistance of the armature; o Insulation resistance & PI of the armature; o DC leakage; o RDT check;  Complete re-wedge  Field re-assembling  Stator re-assembling  Turbine coupling  Closure of the acoustic cabinet  Remove Loto 4 2. TECHNICAL DATA Manufacturer GE Type 7A6 Year 1994 Rated Power 80000 Rated Voltage ( Un ) 11000 Rated Current 1199 Cos phi 0,8 Frequency 50 Hz Rated Speed 3000 Rpm Poles 2 Excitation System Brushless Excitation Volt 500 Total Run hours 92708 5 3. Mechanical checks on disassembling We remove the exciter cover, the shield panels, disconnect the vapor oil discharge fan, the instruments and the cabling of the exciter. We have measured the clearances of the oil deflectors and the air deflector and the position of bearing into their pedestal. See the attached certificates 316221 & 316603. The following pictures show as the generator was before the outage. The generator was completely dirty of oil inside. The oil come from the bearing pedestals, likely the oil is fallen on the floor inside the cabinet and after slipped towards the stator shield, passing down the broken gasket (found completely full of oil and warned) , gone into the generator. The oil was spread all around by the ventilation and was found in any inner parts of the generator. 6 Dirty cover the external part, as CE side as TE side 7 Oil was on the floor inside the acoustic cabinet 8 The connection are in good condition A lot of oil was under the floor of the stator; The exciter is in a good condition, all the surfaces was oiled 9 Exciter Line connections are in good condition but oiled The room of the neutral point was oiled, the surfaces was cleaned from a hard dust, a mix of burned oil and dust 10 Coolers removal The cooler room and the coolers were completely cover by oil. We perform a leakage test on the two coolers, the result is satisfactory. At 4 bar for 1 hour no leakage. 11 Field Removal 12 Bearing The bearing had the lifting oil pipes completely worn. The pads were in good condition. The external surface of the pedestals was very oiled 13 4. Cleaning and material substitution The inner stator casing is been cleaned, the stator winding is been cleaned. All the disassembled parts are been cleaned. The following parts will be changed:  Bearing pads  Oil deflectors  Lifting oil pipes  Stator Wedges  All the Gaskets (either the shield gasket or piping gasket or external cooler gasket) 5. Visual inspection

15 5.2. Field & Exciter The field was completely oiled, a thin layer of oil covers all the component. We cleaned the external surface and where a hand can go. The general condition of the field is now satisfactory, the block under the retaining ring are in position, the connections seem efficient, the ventilation channel are free, the insulation into the slots are in position. The mechanical shrink of the two retaining ring are in good condition, the borescope inspection confirms the same condition of the last inspection. The two journal bearing are in good condition without scratches. See the following pictures: 16 17 18 19 20 Borescope inspection The brazings seem in good condition, the leaves connections are without cracks, the stud nuts are in the correct position. The dark deposit on the insulation (dust and oil spay) has not compromised the insulation between the turns yet. The two radial connection are in satisfactory condition 21

24 6. Electrical tests All the electrical tests have carried out a satisfactory results. See the attached certificates. 7. El Cid test before and after re-wedge The first ElCid performed only on the half lower stator slots. The results are satisfactory, not indication on the core slots where the field printed the lamination, during the removal of the field. The final ElCid , see the attached file, shows a satisfactory results. The small scratches on the 24th slot doesn’t give any indication. 8. Stator Wedges The stator wedges were checked in 2017 by Magic robot. The finding was there is a part of the stator wedges hollow and loose. We performed another wedges mapping, because the field is out. The results are more than 50% of the wedges are under the safe values. The engineer advised to replace all the wedges and the customer accepted the suggestion. Attached the wedges mapping as found before and after the full re-wedge. 25 9. Mechanical re-assembling The generator was re-assembled and the following pictures show as is: The clearances of the gas shield, oil deflectors are checked and are in the following certificates list. Introduction General Electric performed on this generator a major outage as suggested by GEK103566 adding the field extraction after the Magic inspection performed in 2017 where it was find a large area of loose wedges. This generator has worked between 1-1-2015 to 29-11-2019 for 41130 hour, around 8300 hours/year close to a load of 20 MW . The following main actions performed:  Loto on the Generator and steam turbine  Disassembling of the acoustic cabinet  Opening of the coupling  Opening of the stator;  Field extraction;  Electrical Tests: o Insulation resistance & PI on the field and the exciter; o Copper resistance of the generator field and exciter field and armature; o Impedance of the generator field; o Copper resistance of the armature; o Insulation resistance & PI of the armature; o DC leakage; o RDT check;  Complete re-wedge  Field re-assembling  Stator re-assembling  Turbine coupling  Closure of the acoustic cabinet  Remove Loto 4 2. TECHNICAL DATA Manufacturer GE Type 7A6 Year 1994 Rated Power 80000 Rated Voltage ( Un ) 11000 Rated Current 1199 Cos phi 0,8 Frequency 50 Hz Rated Speed 3000 Rpm Poles 2 Excitation System Brushless Excitation Volt 500 Total Run hours 92708 5 3. Mechanical checks on disassembling We remove the exciter cover, the shield panels, disconnect the vapor oil discharge fan, the instruments and the cabling of the exciter. We have measured the clearances of the oil deflectors and the air deflector and the position of bearing into their pedestal. See the attached certificates 316221 & 316603. The following pictures show as the generator was before the outage. The generator was completely dirty of oil inside. The oil come from the bearing pedestals, likely the oil is fallen on the floor inside the cabinet and after slipped towards the stator shield, passing down the broken gasket (found completely full of oil and warned) , gone into the generator. The oil was spread all around by the ventilation and was found in any inner parts of the generator. 6 Dirty cover the external part, as CE side as TE side 7 Oil was on the floor inside the acoustic cabinet 8 The connection are in good condition A lot of oil was under the floor of the stator; The exciter is in a good condition, all the surfaces was oiled 9 Exciter Line connections are in good condition but oiled The room of the neutral point was oiled, the surfaces was cleaned from a hard dust, a mix of burned oil and dust 10 Coolers removal The cooler room and the coolers were completely cover by oil. We perform a leakage test on the two coolers, the result is satisfactory. At 4 bar for 1 hour no leakage. 11 Field Removal 12 Bearing The bearing had the lifting oil pipes completely worn. The pads were in good condition. The external surface of the pedestals was very oiled 13 4. Cleaning and material substitution The inner stator casing is been cleaned, the stator winding is been cleaned. All the disassembled parts are been cleaned. The following parts will be changed:  Bearing pads  Oil deflectors  Lifting oil pipes  Stator Wedges  All the Gaskets (either the shield gasket or piping gasket or external cooler gasket) 5. Visual inspection

15 5.2. Field & Exciter The field was completely oiled, a thin layer of oil covers all the component. We cleaned the external surface and where a hand can go. The general condition of the field is now satisfactory, the block under the retaining ring are in position, the connections seem efficient, the ventilation channel are free, the insulation into the slots are in position. The mechanical shrink of the two retaining ring are in good condition, the borescope inspection confirms the same condition of the last inspection. The two journal bearing are in good condition without scratches. See the following pictures: 16 17 18 19 20 Borescope inspection The brazings seem in good condition, the leaves connections are without cracks, the stud nuts are in the correct position. The dark deposit on the insulation (dust and oil spay) has not compromised the insulation between the turns yet. The two radial connection are in satisfactory condition 21

24 6. Electrical tests All the electrical tests have carried out a satisfactory results. See the attached certificates. 7. El Cid test before and after re-wedge The first ElCid performed only on the half lower stator slots. The results are satisfactory, not indication on the core slots where the field printed the lamination, during the removal of the field. The final ElCid , see the attached file, shows a satisfactory results. The small scratches on the 24th slot doesn’t give any indication. 8. Stator Wedges The stator wedges were checked in 2017 by Magic robot. The finding was there is a part of the stator wedges hollow and loose. We performed another wedges mapping, because the field is out. The results are more than 50% of the wedges are under the safe values. The engineer advised to replace all the wedges and the customer accepted the suggestion. Attached the wedges mapping as found before and after the full re-wedge. 25 9. Mechanical re-assembling The generator was re-assembled and the following pictures show as is: The clearances of the gas shield, oil deflectors are checked and are in the following certificates list.
